rv.q: The cast, under the brisk direction of Jackson Grace Gay, brings lively coloring to all the characters.
'Partnership' charms regardless, offering a gentle reminder about not letting work overtake your life.
Mint's latest, 'Partnership' by Elizabeth Baker, is quite a revelation, both in the quality of the writing and the eye-opening perceptions it reveals about working women more than a century ago.
Partnership is an engaging piece by a writer whose trenchant feminist point of view was allowed to be forgotten for far too long.
As a romantic comedy, this 'Partnership' is regrettably a one-sided affair.

The three plays in the “Meet Miss Baker” Project, "The Price of Thomas Scott" in 2019, "Chains" in 2022 and now "Partnership" in 2023 are quite different. While "Partnership" is the only one you could call a conventional comedy, and a romantic one at that, it offers the least social commentary of the three.
This 'Partnership' simply doesn't meet the Mint's usual high standards.
'Partnership' is still the story of a successful woman running her business into the ground because a man is giving her attention.

...‘Partnership’ more modestly fulfills the Mint’s mission of producing ‘worthwhile plays from the past that have been lost or forgotten’...There are some awkwardly written sequences, but all-around good acting and adept direction by Gay make the journey through Baker’s England a pleasant and rewarding one.
If you're interested in theater history and what are the stepping stones that today's theatrical offerings stand upon, this is a lovely show.
Rarely during the performance's draggy two hours and two minutes do the stakes make us feel much pressure.
The Mint completes its wonderful 'Meet Miss Baker' trilogy with 'Partnership,' another exquisite production of a work by early-twentieth-century playwright and office typist Elizabeth Baker.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Elizabeth Baker revival, with praise for its historical significance and feminist themes but criticism for weak chemistry between leads and a dated romantic plot that undermines its progressive potential.
